items.explanation: Typewriters multiplied paperwork and created clerical jobs — typists and clerks — many filled by women entering office employment in large numbers for the first time. The machines were hand-powered, needing no coal, and had nothing to do with railroads or blacksmithing.
items.fact_source: PD image (Sholes typewriter, manufactured from 1874) + general knowledge: typewriters created clerical jobs, many filled by women — not in u6.md; flagged for audit

option_explanations.A: Correct. The typewriter created office-clerk and typist jobs, drawing many women into office work.
option_explanations.B: Typewriters were hand-operated; they needed no coal or miners.
option_explanations.C: Railroad engineers operated trains, not office machines.
option_explanations.D: Blacksmithing was an unrelated skilled craft.

options: (A) office clerks and typists, including many women entering office work for the first time
(B) coal miners to fuel the machines
(C) railroad engineers
(D) skilled blacksmiths

items.explanation: Big organizations needed administration: someone had to track money, coordinate offices, and handle correspondence across a national market. No law mandated clerk hiring. Factories grew; they did not decline. The assembly line belongs to the next century.
items.fact_source: General knowledge — white-collar growth with corporate scale — not in u6.md; flagged for audit

option_explanations.A: No such law existed; companies hired clerks because they needed them.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Large firms needed administrators to track and coordinate complex operations.
option_explanations.C: Factories grew in this era; they did not decline.
option_explanations.D: The assembly line arrived in the 1910s, after this period.

options: (A) a federal law requiring every company to hire one hundred clerks
(B) the need to administer large business organizations — tracking sales, costs, and correspondence across distance
(C) the decline of factories, which sent workers into offices
(D) the invention of the assembly line

items.explanation: White-collar workers were salaried office employees who generally saw themselves as part of management's world, not labor's — which is why they largely stayed out of unions. The Knights drew laborers, not clerks. Clerks typically earned more and worked cleaner, shorter days than unskilled laborers. They could afford better housing than tenements.
items.fact_source: General knowledge — white-collar characteristics — not in u6.md; flagged for audit

option_explanations.A: The Knights of Labor drew manual laborers; white-collar workers largely stayed out of unions.
option_explanations.B: Clerks generally earned more and worked in better conditions than unskilled laborers.
option_explanations.C: Salaried office workers could afford better housing than crowded tenements.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Salaries, office work, and identification with employers set the white-collar middle class apart.

options: (A) joined the Knights of Labor in greater numbers than any other group
(B) worked longer hours for lower pay than unskilled laborers
(C) lived in tenements alongside recent immigrants
(D) earned salaries rather than hourly wages, worked in offices rather than factories, and identified with their employers rather than with unions

items.explanation: Department stores pioneered fixed marked prices, heavy advertising, and displays aimed at middle-class shoppers — the beginnings of modern consumer culture. Small shops survived alongside them. Variety exploded rather than declined. Retailing stayed private.
items.fact_source: General knowledge — department stores, fixed prices, consumer culture, 1870s–90s — not in u6.md; flagged for audit

option_explanations.A: Small neighborhood shops continued to operate alongside the big stores.
option_explanations.B: Department stores vastly increased the variety of goods on offer.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Fixed prices, advertising, and middle-class shopping define early consumer culture.
option_explanations.D: Retailing remained entirely in private hands.

options: (A) the end of all small neighborhood shops
(B) a decline in the variety of goods available to shoppers
(C) the rise of consumer culture: fixed prices, advertised goods, and shopping as a middle-class activity
(D) the government's takeover of retail trade
items.stem: Large department stores appeared in American cities in the 1870s–1890s. They best illustrate which change in American life?

items.explanation: Catalogs only worked because railroads and the post could carry goods cheaply to remote buyers. Automobiles came later and are irrelevant here. Stores stayed private. Catalogs sold factory-made goods; they depended on factory production, not its end.
items.fact_source: General knowledge — mail-order catalogs (1870s–90s) — not in u6.md; flagged for audit; partial link: u6.md §The story — railroad track 35,000→190,000 miles

option_explanations.A: Correct. Cheap long-distance delivery by rail and post made mail-order possible.
option_explanations.B: Automobiles arrived decades later; catalogs predated them.
option_explanations.C: Stores and catalog companies were private businesses.
option_explanations.D: Catalogs sold factory-made goods — they depended on factories, not their disappearance.

options: (A) the railroad network and a national postal system that could deliver goods cheaply over long distances
(B) the invention of the automobile
(C) government ownership of all stores
(D) the end of factory production

items.explanation: Mass production created a new problem: when many factories make nearly identical soap, producers must convince shoppers to pick their brand — hence mass advertising. No law required advertising. Literacy was rising, and ads combined images with text. Soap was ancient; what was new was branding it for a national market.
items.fact_source: PD trade-card advertisement, ca. 1880 (stimulus) + general knowledge: mass production → brand advertising — flagged for audit

option_explanations.A: No law ever required products to be advertised.
option_explanations.B: Literacy was rising in this era, and advertisements combined pictures with text.
option_explanations.C: Soap was an ancient product; national branding of it was the novelty.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Identical mass-produced goods forced producers to compete through brand advertising.

options: (A) the government required every product to be advertised
(B) most Americans could not read, so pictures replaced all text
(C) soap was a new invention of the 1880s
(D) factories were producing identical goods in large quantities and needed to persuade consumers to choose their brand

items.explanation: When factories turned out goods in volume, prices fell — prices fell and output soared — so middle-class households could buy things earlier generations considered luxuries. Prices fell rather than rose. Advertising grew with mass production rather than ending. Goods became more abundant, not scarcer.
items.fact_source: u6.md §The story — 'Prices fell and output soared' + general knowledge (consumer culture) — partially flagged

option_explanations.A: Mass production lowered prices; it did not raise them.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Falling prices brought former luxuries within reach of salaried households.
option_explanations.C: Advertising expanded alongside mass production; it did not end.
option_explanations.D: Mass production made goods abundant, not scarce.

options: (A) Mass production raised prices, so only the rich could buy manufactured goods.
(B) Mass production lowered the price of goods, putting items once considered luxuries within reach of salaried households.
(C) Mass production ended all advertising.
(D) Mass production made goods scarcer and more precious.

items.explanation: Cheap, fast streetcar lines let middle-class workers live beyond walking distance of downtown and still reach their jobs — the physical basis of the early suburb. People kept walking. Streetcars were urban passenger transit, not long-distance freight. Horses remained common for years afterward.
items.fact_source: PD illustration (Street Railway Review, 1891) + general knowledge: streetcars → suburban commuting — not in u6.md; flagged for audit

option_explanations.A: People continued to walk; streetcars supplemented walking rather than ending it.
option_explanations.B: Streetcars carried city passengers, not cross-country freight.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Streetcars made commuting from outlying residential areas practical.
option_explanations.D: Horse-drawn vehicles remained common well after streetcars spread.

options: (A) the end of all walking in American cities
(B) farmers to ship wheat by streetcar across the country
(C) early suburbs, as middle-class families could live farther from city centers and commute to work
(D) the immediate disappearance of horse-drawn vehicles
